content.text:
**No — nothing in forgemark sends "forgemark" in a User-Agent.** There isn't a single User-Agent reference in the repo's own code. What actually goes over the wire today:

- **Git smart-HTTP traffic** (clone/fetch/push, the bulk of the load) goes through go-git v6, whose HTTP transport stamps every request with `User-Agent: go-git/6.x` (`plumbing/transport/http/common.go:92` via `capability.DefaultAgent()`). So on the server side, forgemark runs look identical to any other go-git client.
- **Forgemark's own direct requests** set no User-Agent at all, so they get Go's stdlib default, `Go-http-client/1.1` (or `/2.0`):
  - the OAuth token POST in `internal/bench/creds.go:206`
  - the endpoint probe GET in `internal/bench/endpoint.go:73`

If you want requests identifiable as forgemark, there are two easy paths:

1. **Zero-code:** go-git's `DefaultAgent()` honors a `GO_GIT_USER_AGENT_EXTRA` env var, so exporting something like `forgemark/<version>` yields `User-Agent: go-git/6.x forgemark/<version>` on all git traffic (but not the two direct HTTP calls).
2. **One-point code fix:** everything — git ops and the direct calls — flows through the single shared client built in `newHTTPClient` (`internal/bench/runner.go:277`), because the agents pass it into go-git via `gitclient.WithHTTPClient(a.httpc)` (`internal/bench/agent.go:127`). Wrapping that client's transport in a RoundTripper that sets (or appends to) the User-Agent would tag every request forgemark makes, including overriding go-git's header since the RoundTripper runs last.

Happy to implement option 2 if you want it.

That confirms the picture, and both fix paths are user-owned commands, so here's where things stand.

**Diagnosis:** Your two accounts see disjoint halves of the same repo. The CLI context (`us.auth.entire.io`, @kramuenke — your personal GitHub identity) sees *only* trail 4 and genuinely cannot find trails 1–3 (`entire trail show 3` → "no trail found", `trail list --status any` → just #4, with no author filter and limit 10). Your browser account sees trails 1–3 but not 4. So trail 4 landed in a project record that @kramuenke's login maps this repo to, while your UI account is looking at a different project for the same repo — the numbering continuing at 4 suggests the server shares a per-repo counter even across that boundary.

**To fix it** (these are account-management commands the CLI reserves for you to run yourself):

1. See which project each side maps to: `entire project list` (and `entire project get`) — run once as-is and, if you want to compare, once with `--context us.auth.partial.to` for whatever your other login sees.
2. Then either grant your UI account/org access to the project trail 4 is in: `entire grant project ...` (see `entire agent-help grant project` for exact args), or move the CLI onto the org/project your team actually uses (`entire org ...`) so future trails land where everyone looks.

If you'd rather just relocate the trail: once your CLI context points at the right org/project, say the word and I'll delete trail 4 and recreate it there — the branch and commit are untouched by any of this, so nothing else needs redoing.

Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
